Apr 14

Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Yes, but call it what it is: choreography, not orchestration. gh-aw has no DAG, no pipeline engine, no "workflow of workflows" primitive. Agents hand off through GitHub events: one agent labels an issue, the label triggers the next agent, that agent assigns to Copilot coding agent, the resulting PR triggers the reviewer. Loose coupling all the way down. That's the whole trick, and it's also why Peli's factory scales to 100+ workflows without collapsing.

The concrete chain for spec → ship → review looks like this:

Spec agent (on: issues.opened, label needs-spec) reads a rough idea, rewrites it as a structured spec with acceptance criteria, posts it back on the issue, swaps the label to needs-plan.
Planner agent (on: issues.labeled [needs-plan]) breaks the spec into a task list, files sub-issues via create-issue, adds ready-for-implementation to each.
Implementer handoff (on: issues.labeled [ready-for-implementation]) uses the assign-to-agent safe output to hand the sub-issue to Copilot's cloud coding agent. This is the one step where real code gets written, and it's deliberately not a gh-aw agent because Copilot coding agent is the right tool for multi-file edits with CI feedback loops.
Reviewer agent (on: pull_request.opened) reads the diff, checks it against the original spec (pulled from the parent issue), posts a structured review, labels the PR ai-reviewed or needs-changes.
Gatekeeper agent (optional, on: pull_request.labeled [needs-changes]) pings the author on Slack via MCP, or re-assigns back to Copilot coding agent for a fix pass.
Three things that will bite you if you don't plan for them:

State between phases lives in issues, not memory. Each agent starts cold. The spec must be written back to the issue body or a comment so the planner can read it. Use repo-memory only for genuinely cross-run state like "which issues have I already seen." Issues are your database.

The review loop is where most factories fail. If your reviewer agent is too strict you get infinite rework loops; too loose and it's theater. Budget real time to tune the reviewer's prompt against 20-30 real PRs before you trust it. This is harness engineering work, not prompt work.

Non-determinism means you need a human circuit breaker. Add a human-review label that halts the chain at any step. The factory should be pauseable by any developer who sees it going sideways. Peli's team calls this the "emergency stop," and every production chain has one.

Honest take: for TV 2's platform team, the spec → plan → review chain is the right first factory to build because PMs and platform engineers already think in those phases. The implementation step is the weakest link (Copilot coding agent still produces PRs that need rework), so start by automating the bookends: spec refinement and PR review. Leave the middle for humans until you trust the tooling. That's a working agent factory in two workflows, not five, and it ships next week instead of next quarter.

How many of these agentic workflow agents are already in the gh-aw-workflows repo?

Inventoried available workflows and mapped them to user's development chain
Inventoried available workflows and mapped them to user's development chain
Roughly 20 in the public sample pack (githubnext/agentics) and 50+ in Peli's Agent Factory demonstrator. Two different numbers because they're two different things: the sample pack is the curated, reusable set you can gh aw add directly; Peli's factory is the living showcase running on GitHub Next's own repos.

Here's what's actually in githubnext/agentics right now, mapped to your spec→review chain:

Direct hits for your chain:

/plan — breaks issues into actionable sub-tasks (your planner step, basically done)
/pr-fix — analyzes failing CI, pushes fixes to the PR branch (your rework loop)
issue-triage — labels new issues (your front door)
repo-assist — the "backlog burner" generalist that triages, investigates, comments, fixes bugs
Adjacent and useful:

ci-doctor — investigates CI failures, files reports (feeds your reviewer)
ci-coach — optimizes CI for speed/cost
ai-moderator — spam and AI-slop detection (gate on incoming issues)
archie — generates Mermaid diagrams of issue/PR relationships
repo-ask — research assistant for repo questions
daily-repo-status — the hello-world reporting agent
weekly-repository-map — ASCII tree map of repo structure
daily-documentation-updater, regular-documentation-update, agentic-wiki-writer — docs maintenance
daily-accessibility-review, multi-device-docs-tester, daily-adhoc-qa — QA agents
tech-content-editorial-board — editorial review of technical content
dependabot-pr-bundler, dependabot-issue-bundler — dependency hygiene
What's missing from your spec→review chain and you'll need to write yourself:

A spec refinement agent that takes a rough issue and rewrites it with acceptance criteria. Nothing off-the-shelf.
A PR reviewer agent that checks diffs against the original spec. pr-fix fixes CI, it doesn't review intent. This is the one that matters most for your factory and it's the one you have to build.
So the honest scorecard: the bookends of your chain (planner, rework) are already solved by /plan and /pr-fix. The middle bits (spec refinement, intent-based review) don't exist yet and that's where your harness engineering time goes. Which is actually fine, because those are the two steps where TV 2's platform context matters most, and a generic agent couldn't do them well anyway.

Start command:

bash
gh aw add githubnext/agentics/plan
gh aw add githubnext/agentics/pr-fix
gh aw add githubnext/agentics/issue-triage
Three commands, three working agents, and you're halfway to your factory before lunch.

Synthesized skills architecture with agent factory choreography patterns
Synthesized skills architecture with agent factory choreography patterns
Your skills repo is the missing layer. The gh-aw factory gives you choreography between agents. Your skills give each agent a better harness. Combined, you get the two-loop model you wrote about on LinkedIn, running in production on GitHub Actions.

Here's the mapping:

Your three skills, translated to the factory
plan-interview is literally the spec refinement agent I flagged as missing from your chain. It already does structured intent capture before planning. Port it to a gh-aw workflow triggered on issues.labeled [needs-spec], paste the SKILL.md instructions into the workflow body, add safe-outputs: update-issue so it writes the refined spec back to the issue body, then swaps the label to needs-plan. That hands off to githubnext/agentics/plan. You just completed the front half of your chain using one existing skill and one existing sample workflow.

self-improvement is the outer loop. This is the one that matters most and the one nobody else is building. In your local Claude Code setup it uses PostToolUse hooks. gh-aw has no hooks, but it has cache-memory and repo-memory tools plus a .learnings/ directory pattern that can be committed to the repo. The translation: a scheduled meta-agent that runs nightly, reads the last 24 hours of workflow run logs via gh aw logs, extracts failure patterns, and opens a PR updating AGENTS.md or the relevant workflow's markdown body with the new guardrails. Learnings become permanent evals the moment they land in a committed file. This is harness engineering as continuous integration, running on GitHub Actions, authored in your own skill.

dx-data-navigator becomes the reviewer's context source. Wire it in two ways: if DX has an MCP server, add it to the workflow's mcp-servers: block; if not, wrap the CLI in a custom MCP server and host it behind your firewall. The PR review agent then pulls actual DORA metrics and PR cycle time data when judging a change, instead of reviewing in a vacuum. This is what separates your reviewer from every generic AI reviewer on the market.

The upgraded chain
issues.opened
  └─> spec-refiner (plan-interview skill)
        writes refined spec back to issue, labels needs-plan
  └─> /plan (githubnext/agentics/plan)
        creates sub-issues labeled ready-for-implementation
  └─> assign-to-agent (Copilot coding agent cloud)
        opens PR
  └─> pr-reviewer (custom, uses dx-data-navigator via MCP)
        reviews against original spec + DX context
  └─> /pr-fix (githubnext/agentics/pr-fix) if needs-changes
        pushes fix to branch, loops
  └─> [nightly] self-improvement meta-agent
        reads run logs, commits learnings to AGENTS.md
Five specialist agents, three from your skills, two from the sample pack. That's the whole factory.

The concrete "import skills into gh-aw" mechanism
gh-aw workflows are markdown with frontmatter. Your SKILL.md files are markdown with frontmatter. The formats are not identical but the content is directly transferable. Two options:

Option A, the fast one. Copy the instructions section of each SKILL.md into the body of a gh-aw workflow file. Add gh-aw frontmatter (triggers, permissions, safe-outputs). Done in 10 minutes per skill. Loses the ability to update skills centrally.

Option B, the proper one. Create a pskoett/tv2-agentics repo structured as a gh-aw sample pack. Each workflow imports shared instruction snippets from a .github/aw/shared/ directory that mirrors your skill structure. Use gh-aw's imports: frontmatter field to pull them in at compile time. Now your skills library and your agent factory are the same repo, and gh aw update keeps every consuming repo current. This is the TV 2 version of Peli's agent factory.

Go with Option B. It matches your thesis that skills are the new software and it's also how you'd sell this internally at TV 2.

The self-improvement meta-agent, specifically
This one is worth writing out because it's the piece that makes your factory actually improve over time:

markdown
---
on:
  schedule: daily at 2am utc+1
timeout-minutes: 15
permissions:
  actions: read
  contents: read
tools:
  github:
    toolsets: [actions, repos]
  cache-memory:
  bash:
    allowed: ["gh aw logs", "gh aw audit", "gh run list"]
safe-outputs:
  create-pull-request:
    max: 1
    title-prefix: "[learnings] "
    labels: [self-improvement, automation]
---

# Self-Improvement Meta-Agent

You are the outer loop of a two-loop agent improvement architecture.

## Your job
Read the last 24 hours of agentic workflow runs. For each failure or
degraded-quality output, extract the root cause. Encode the fix as a
permanent addition to the relevant workflow's instructions or to the
shared AGENTS.md file.

## Process
1. List all runs from `.github/workflows/*.md` files in the last 24h
2. For each failed or flagged run, read the logs
3. Categorize: prompt issue, tool issue, context issue, data issue
4. For prompt and context issues, draft a specific instruction addition
5. Open a single PR that updates the relevant markdown files
6. Include the failing run IDs in the PR description as evidence
7. Each learning must be a regression test: specific enough that future
   runs can be checked against it

If no failures or degraded outputs exist, call noop and explain.

## What counts as a learning
A learning is not "be more careful." A learning is a specific, checkable
rule: "When triaging issues that mention 'CI', always check the last 3
failed runs before labeling as bug." That's encodable. That's a test.
That's your outer loop, running nightly, on GitHub Actions, authored as a skill, filing PRs that improve the other agents. The flywheel you described in your harness engineering post, but shipped.

Honest take on what this unlocks
You are one weekend of work away from a working agent factory that is genuinely differentiated from what GitHub ships out of the box. The three things that make it yours and not Peli's:

plan-interview as a front door. Nobody else is doing structured intent capture before planning. Most factories skip straight to "break the issue into tasks" and get garbage in, garbage out.
The self-improvement outer loop. Peli's factory has a health manager that files issues when agents fail. Yours will file PRs that fix the underlying instructions. That's a different quality of loop.
DX data in the reviewer. Using real DORA metrics as reviewer context is the kind of thing only a platform team with DX already wired up can do. This is TV 2's unfair advantage and you already have the CLI for it.
One thing to watch. Your skills were written for local agent loops with hooks. gh-aw's execution model is ephemeral containers with safe outputs. Some of your skill content assumes state that doesn't persist across runs. Specifically, the self-improvement skill's .learnings/ directory needs to be a committed path in the target repo, not a local scratch directory. Audit each skill for local-loop assumptions before porting and you'll save yourself a debugging cycle.

How to ship it tomorrow morning:

bash
# 1. Create the repo
gh repo create pskoett/tv2-agentics --public --source=. --push

# 2. In any target repo where you want the chain

The installer adds three workflows from this pack and three from githubnext/agentics (plan, pr-fix, issue-triage), compiles everything, and tells you what secrets are still missing.

Three things to know before you push:

The DX MCP URL in tv2-reviewer.md is a placeholder. I used https://dx-mcp.tv2.dk/mcp as a reasonable guess. Swap it for the real TV 2 DX Data Cloud endpoint, or remove the mcp-servers block entirely if you want to ship without it and add it in a second pass. The reviewer degrades gracefully when the MCP server is missing.
self-improvement-meta.md assumes gh aw logs, gh aw audit, and gh aw status are available in the bash allowlist. Those commands ship with the gh-aw extension, but whether they work inside a sandboxed workflow run depends on how the runner is configured. If they fail, fall back to gh run list --json and parse run metadata from GitHub's API directly. Worth testing on the first nightly run.
spec-refiner uses slash_command: /review on the reviewer but no slash command on itself. That's deliberate: the front door should trigger on labels, not on commands. If you want manual triggering during testing, add workflow_dispatch: to its on: block and recompile.
The honest caveats:

This is scaffolding, not production code. The instruction bodies are good first drafts but the real quality will come from running them against real issues and letting self-improvement-meta tighten them over two or three weeks.
The plan-interview port loses the interactivity of the original skill. A single-shot agent cannot interview a user. I worked around this by having it answer the interview questions itself from context and flag anything it is not confident about with **NEEDS HUMAN INPUT**. You may find that some issues need a preparatory human comment before needs-spec gets applied, just to give the agent enough context.
I did not port intent-framed-agent or context-surfing. Those skills assume a live session with a context window Claude can monitor. gh-aw's ephemeral single-shot runs break the assumption. If you want something equivalent, the closest thing is adding a "check your intent against the plan file every 3 tool calls" instruction inside each workflow body. Let me know and I'll add that pattern.
What to do next:

Push this to github.com/pskoett/tv2-agentics, then run ./install-chain.sh against a throwaway test repo. Open three test issues labeled needs-spec: one trivial bug, one multi-component feature, one refactor. Watch how the chain handles each. The trivial bug should get a noop with a short comment. The feature should get a full plan file. The refactor is where you'll see the rough edges and start feeding improvements back into the workflow bodies.

That's the feedback loop. Fourteen days of real runs will teach you more than another fourteen hours of planning.

Examined engine compatibility and realized the port was unnecessarily elaborate
Examined engine compatibility and realized the port was unnecessarily elaborate
No reason at all. And your question is pointing at something I should have flagged before I built the port: committing your skills directory directly into the target repo is simpler than what I just did.

Here's the mechanics:

Claude Code and Codex engines auto-discover skills. Both scan the filesystem for SKILL.md files at runtime. Claude Code reads from .claude/skills/ and similar locations. Codex scans .agents/skills/ from cwd up to repo root. If you commit skills/ into the target repo and use either engine, the skills light up with zero porting.

Copilot is the outlier. It has no native skill discovery. It reads AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md and that's it. So for Copilot you either inline the skill content (what I did) or reference the skill files from AGENTS.md and let Copilot's file-reading tools pull them in on demand.

Three caveats regardless of engine:

Skills with scripts need matching bash allowlists. Your self-improvement skill has shell scripts in scripts/. For those to run inside gh-aw, the workflow frontmatter has to include those commands in the bash: allowed: block. Instruction-only skills are free.
Skills with MCP servers need frontmatter declarations. If a skill bundles an MCP server, gh-aw won't auto-wire it. You declare it in the workflow's mcp-servers: block like we did for DX data.
Prompt injection surface. Skills get loaded into the agent's context as instructions. In a TV 2 internal repo where the platform team owns the skills, this is fine. In a public repo accepting contributions, it's a vector.
Which means my port was overbuilt. The simpler architecture for your factory:

target-repo/
├── skills/                          ← commit your full skills dir as-is
│   ├── plan-interview/
│   ├── self-improvement/
│   ├── dx-data-navigator/
│   ├── intent-framed-agent/         ← now these work too
│   └── context-surfing/             ← and these
├── AGENTS.md                        ← tells the agent to discover skills/
└── .github/workflows/
    ├── spec-refiner.md              ← short body: "use the plan-interview skill"
    ├── tv2-reviewer.md              ← short body: "use dx-data-navigator skill"
    └── self-improvement-meta.md     ← short body: "use self-improvement skill"
The workflow bodies shrink to maybe 20 lines each. The skills stay in their canonical repo layout. You can test them locally with Claude Code, ship them as gh-aw workflows, and reuse them in Codex CLI. Single source of truth.

And the part that actually unlocks: intent-framed-agent and context-surfing stop being unportable. I told you earlier those skills assume a live session with a monitorable context window. That's still true for the "monitor context health mid-run" use case. But the intent framing itself, the structured drift checks, the exit-with-handoff pattern, those all work fine in a single-shot gh-aw run because the agent reads the skill, follows the instructions, and produces an artifact. The "live monitoring" part is what doesn't translate. The "structured discipline" part does.

Honest take on what to do with what I built:

Keep tv2-agentics as the workflow shell (frontmatter, triggers, safe outputs, handoff labels). Gut the inlined skill content from the workflow bodies. Replace it with short references like:

markdown
# Spec Refiner

You are running the plan-interview skill from `skills/plan-interview/SKILL.md`
in this repository. Read that file now and follow its process.

Your output must land as a plan file in `docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md` and
you must open a PR with it via the safe-outputs below.

## Handoff
[the gh-aw specific stuff: labels to swap, PR structure, noop conditions]
That's 15 lines instead of 150. The skill stays in your canonical repo. Updates propagate. And it works for Claude, Codex, and Copilot alike because you're not relying on auto-discovery, you're telling the agent to read a specific file path.

Want me to refactor the pack along these lines? It's a 20-minute job. The result is a thinner tv2-agentics that acts as the gh-aw adapter layer, plus a convention that pskoett-ai-skills gets vendored (or submoduled) into any repo that runs the chain. That matches your "skills are the new software" thesis way better than the inlined version does.

Do it make the repo changes and make the files like before

Streamlined workflow files and consolidated skill logic
Streamlined workflow files and consolidated skill logic
Refactored. Here's what changed and why it matters.

Workflow bodies shrank dramatically. The three workflows went from ~430 lines of inlined skill logic to 287 lines total, and most of what's left is gh-aw-specific plumbing (frontmatter, safe outputs, bash allowlists, MCP config) that genuinely can't live in a skill file. The actual agent process now lives exclusively in skills/ where it belongs.

spec-refiner.md is now 63 lines. It says "read skills/plan-interview/SKILL.md and follow it, adapt for single-shot per AGENTS.md rule 1, then hand off with these labels." That's the entire shell.

AGENTS.md got a new section: "Adapting skills for single-shot gh-aw runs". Four rules cover the scenarios where a skill assumes something gh-aw can't provide:

Interview-style skills → simulate from context, flag unknowns
Hook-based skills → apply logic at natural phase boundaries
Session-state skills → run discipline as self-checks
Script-bundled skills → declare in bash allowlist
This centralizes the translation logic. Every workflow points at these rules instead of re-explaining the adaptation per workflow. When you figure out a better way to adapt an interactive skill to single-shot, you update one file.

install-chain.sh now vendors skills first. It calls npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills, handles the "skills already exist" case with an update prompt, seeds .learnings/ if missing, copies AGENTS.md if not present, then adds the six workflows and compiles. Colored output, proper error handling, no surprises.

skills/ directory has a README but no actual skills. This is intentional. The tv2-agentics source repo shouldn't contain the vendored skills because that would duplicate them. The skills land in the target repo at install time via npx. The README in skills/ explains the convention so anyone browsing the repo understands why it's empty.

intent-framed-agent and context-surfing now get used. I couldn't port them before because they assumed live sessions. With the thin-shell architecture, tv2-reviewer references intent-framed-agent for drift checking against the plan, and future workflows can pull in context-surfing as a self-check discipline. The skills stay canonical. The workflows just say "read this and apply it."

What to do now:

tar -xzf tv2-agentics.tar.gz

One thing worth noting before you ship this publicly: npx skills add is the command from your pskoett-ai-skills README, but I haven't verified whether that CLI is actually published to npm or if it's aspirational. If the skills CLI doesn't exist yet, the install script will fail at step 1. Quick fix: replace the npx skills add call with git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills /tmp/skills && cp -r /tmp/skills/skills ./skills && rm -rf /tmp/skills. Same outcome, no npx dependency. Your call which pattern you want to commit to.

Evaluated changelog implications for agent routing and workflow automation
Evaluated changelog implications for agent routing and workflow automation
Read the changelog. This is a real shift. Let me be precise about what changes and what doesn't.

What the changelog definitely enables:

Claude and Codex are now first-class cloud coding agents on github.com, at parity with Copilot cloud agent, with model selection at task kickoff. Access is bundled with the Copilot subscription, no separate ANTHROPIC_API_KEY required. For Claude you can pick Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.5, or Sonnet 4.5. Admin has to flip the policy on for Business/Enterprise, and the repo owner enables it in Settings > Copilot > Cloud agent.

What this means for your factory specifically:

The middle of your chain, the implementer step, just got a major upgrade. Your plan was:

/plan creates sub-issues → assign-to-agent → Copilot cloud agent → PR
Now it can be:

/plan creates sub-issues → assign-to-agent → Claude Opus 4.6 → PR
Two things follow from this, and one of them is actually significant for you personally:

Claude Opus 4.6 for complex implementations is a measurable quality upgrade over Copilot cloud agent's default. Opus is widely stronger at multi-file refactors, intricate logic, and sticking to a spec. For TV 2's platform work where context and precision matter, this is the right default for anything non-trivial.
Your skills were designed for Claude Code. They now run on their native runtime for the implementer step. The plan-interview skill's output, the intent framing discipline, the simplify-and-harden pass, all of it was tuned against Claude's reasoning patterns. Running it through Claude Opus at the implementer step means the skills execute on the runtime they were shaped by. That's better fidelity than any amount of porting could give you.
What I am NOT sure about, and you should verify before building on it:

Whether gh-aw's assign-to-agent safe output currently supports routing to Claude or Codex, or if it still only targets Copilot cloud agent. The web UI has the model picker. The gh-aw safe output's status is unclear from what I can find. If gh-aw hasn't caught up yet, the routing for the PoC has to be:

Automated assignment via assign-to-agent → lands on Copilot cloud agent (current behavior)
Or manual assignment via the web UI → you pick Claude Opus 4.6 yourself when starting the task

Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Yes, but call it what it is: choreography, not orchestration. gh-aw has no DAG, no pipeline engine, no "workflow of workflows" primitive. Agents hand off through GitHub events: one agent labels an issue, the label triggers the next agent, that agent assigns to Copilot coding agent, the resulting PR triggers the reviewer. Loose coupling all the way down. That's the whole trick, and it's also why Peli's factory scales to 100+ workflows without collapsing.

The concrete chain for spec → ship → review looks like this:

Spec agent (on: issues.opened, label needs-spec) reads a rough idea, rewrites it as a structured spec with acceptance criteria, posts it back on the issue, swaps the label to needs-plan.
Planner agent (on: issues.labeled [needs-plan]) breaks the spec into a task list, files sub-issues via create-issue, adds ready-for-implementation to each.
Implementer handoff (on: issues.labeled [ready-for-implementation]) uses the assign-to-agent safe output to hand the sub-issue to Copilot's cloud coding agent. This is the one step where real code gets written, and it's deliberately not a gh-aw agent because Copilot coding agent is the right tool for multi-file edits with CI feedback loops.
Reviewer agent (on: pull_request.opened) reads the diff, checks it against the original spec (pulled from the parent issue), posts a structured review, labels the PR ai-reviewed or needs-changes.
Gatekeeper agent (optional, on: pull_request.labeled [needs-changes]) pings the author on Slack via MCP, or re-assigns back to Copilot coding agent for a fix pass.
Three things that will bite you if you don't plan for them:

State between phases lives in issues, not memory. Each agent starts cold. The spec must be written back to the issue body or a comment so the planner can read it. Use repo-memory only for genuinely cross-run state like "which issues have I already seen." Issues are your database.

The review loop is where most factories fail. If your reviewer agent is too strict you get infinite rework loops; too loose and it's theater. Budget real time to tune the reviewer's prompt against 20-30 real PRs before you trust it. This is harness engineering work, not prompt work.

Non-determinism means you need a human circuit breaker. Add a human-review label that halts the chain at any step. The factory should be pauseable by any developer who sees it going sideways. Peli's team calls this the "emergency stop," and every production chain has one.

Honest take: for TV 2's platform team, the spec → plan → review chain is the right first factory to build because PMs and platform engineers already think in those phases. The implementation step is the weakest link (Copilot coding agent still produces PRs that need rework), so start by automating the bookends: spec refinement and PR review. Leave the middle for humans until you trust the tooling. That's a working agent factory in two workflows, not five, and it ships next week instead of next quarter.

You are the outer loop of a two-loop agent improvement architecture.

Read the last 24 hours of agentic workflow runs. For each failure or

2. For each failed or flagged run, read the logs

Here's the mechanics:

Claude Code and Codex engines auto-discover skills. Both scan the filesystem for SKILL.md files at runtime. Claude Code reads from .claude/skills/ and similar locations. Codex scans .agents/skills/ from cwd up to repo root. If you commit skills/ into the target repo and use either engine, the skills light up with zero porting.

Copilot is the outlier. It has no native skill discovery. It reads AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md and that's it. So for Copilot you either inline the skill content (what I did) or reference the skill files from AGENTS.md and let Copilot's file-reading tools pull them in on demand.

Three caveats regardless of engine:

Skills with scripts need matching bash allowlists. Your self-improvement skill has shell scripts in scripts/. For those to run inside gh-aw, the workflow frontmatter has to include those commands in the bash: allowed: block. Instruction-only skills are free.
Skills with MCP servers need frontmatter declarations. If a skill bundles an MCP server, gh-aw won't auto-wire it. You declare it in the workflow's mcp-servers: block like we did for DX data.
Prompt injection surface. Skills get loaded into the agent's context as instructions. In a TV 2 internal repo where the platform team owns the skills, this is fine. In a public repo accepting contributions, it's a vector.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Yes, but call it what it is: choreography, not orchestration. gh-aw has no DAG, no pipeline engine, no "workflow of workflows" primitive. Agents hand off through GitHub events: one agent labels an issue, the label triggers the next agent, that agent assigns to Copilot coding agent, the resulting PR triggers the reviewer. Loose coupling all the way down. That's the whole trick, and it's also why Peli's factory scales to 100+ workflows without collapsing.

The concrete chain for spec → ship → review looks like this:

Spec agent (on: issues.opened, label needs-spec) reads a rough idea, rewrites it as a structured spec with acceptance criteria, posts it back on the issue, swaps the label to needs-plan.
Planner agent (on: issues.labeled [needs-plan]) breaks the spec into a task list, files sub-issues via create-issue, adds ready-for-implementation to each.
Implementer handoff (on: issues.labeled [ready-for-implementation]) uses the assign-to-agent safe output to hand the sub-issue to Copilot's cloud coding agent. This is the one step where real code gets written, and it's deliberately not a gh-aw agent because Copilot coding agent is the right tool for multi-file edits with CI feedback loops.
Reviewer agent (on: pull_request.opened) reads the diff, checks it against the original spec (pulled from the parent issue), posts a structured review, labels the PR ai-reviewed or needs-changes.
Gatekeeper agent (optional, on: pull_request.labeled [needs-changes]) pings the author on Slack via MCP, or re-assigns back to Copilot coding agent for a fix pass.
Three things that will bite you if you don't plan for them:

State between phases lives in issues, not memory. Each agent starts cold. The spec must be written back to the issue body or a comment so the planner can read it. Use repo-memory only for genuinely cross-run state like "which issues have I already seen." Issues are your database.

The review loop is where most factories fail. If your reviewer agent is too strict you get infinite rework loops; too loose and it's theater. Budget real time to tune the reviewer's prompt against 20-30 real PRs before you trust it. This is harness engineering work, not prompt work.

Non-determinism means you need a human circuit breaker. Add a human-review label that halts the chain at any step. The factory should be pauseable by any developer who sees it going sideways. Peli's team calls this the "emergency stop," and every production chain has one.

Honest take: for TV 2's platform team, the spec → plan → review chain is the right first factory to build because PMs and platform engineers already think in those phases. The implementation step is the weakest link (Copilot coding agent still produces PRs that need rework), so start by automating the bookends: spec refinement and PR review. Leave the middle for humans until you trust the tooling. That's a working agent factory in two workflows, not five, and it ships next week instead of next quarter.

Synthesized skills architecture with agent factory choreography patterns
Your skills repo is the missing layer. The gh-aw factory gives you choreography between agents. Your skills give each agent a better harness. Combined, you get the two-loop model you wrote about on LinkedIn, running in production on GitHub Actions.

Here's the mapping:

Your three skills, translated to the factory
plan-interview is literally the spec refinement agent I flagged as missing from your chain. It already does structured intent capture before planning. Port it to a gh-aw workflow triggered on issues.labeled [needs-spec], paste the SKILL.md instructions into the workflow body, add safe-outputs: update-issue so it writes the refined spec back to the issue body, then swaps the label to needs-plan. That hands off to githubnext/agentics/plan. You just completed the front half of your chain using one existing skill and one existing sample workflow.

self-improvement is the outer loop. This is the one that matters most and the one nobody else is building. In your local Claude Code setup it uses PostToolUse hooks. gh-aw has no hooks, but it has cache-memory and repo-memory tools plus a .learnings/ directory pattern that can be committed to the repo. The translation: a scheduled meta-agent that runs nightly, reads the last 24 hours of workflow run logs via gh aw logs, extracts failure patterns, and opens a PR updating AGENTS.md or the relevant workflow's markdown body with the new guardrails. Learnings become permanent evals the moment they land in a committed file. This is harness engineering as continuous integration, running on GitHub Actions, authored in your own skill.

dx-data-navigator becomes the reviewer's context source. Wire it in two ways: if DX has an MCP server, add it to the workflow's mcp-servers: block; if not, wrap the CLI in a custom MCP server and host it behind your firewall. The PR review agent then pulls actual DORA metrics and PR cycle time data when judging a change, instead of reviewing in a vacuum. This is what separates your reviewer from every generic AI reviewer on the market.

The upgraded chain
issues.opened
  └─> spec-refiner (plan-interview skill)
        writes refined spec back to issue, labels needs-plan
  └─> /plan (githubnext/agentics/plan)
        creates sub-issues labeled ready-for-implementation
  └─> assign-to-agent (Copilot coding agent cloud)
        opens PR
  └─> pr-reviewer (custom, uses dx-data-navigator via MCP)
        reviews against original spec + DX context
  └─> /pr-fix (githubnext/agentics/pr-fix) if needs-changes
        pushes fix to branch, loops
  └─> [nightly] self-improvement meta-agent
        reads run logs, commits learnings to AGENTS.md
Five specialist agents, three from your skills, two from the sample pack. That's the whole factory.

The concrete "import skills into gh-aw" mechanism
gh-aw workflows are markdown with frontmatter. Your SKILL.md files are markdown with frontmatter. The formats are not identical but the content is directly transferable. Two options:

Option A, the fast one. Copy the instructions section of each SKILL.md into the body of a gh-aw workflow file. Add gh-aw frontmatter (triggers, permissions, safe-outputs). Done in 10 minutes per skill. Loses the ability to update skills centrally.

Validated end-to-end agent factory feasibility through event-driven choreography
Yes, but call it what it is: choreography, not orchestration. gh-aw has no DAG, no pipeline engine, no "workflow of workflows" primitive. Agents hand off through GitHub events: one agent labels an issue, the label triggers the next agent, that agent assigns to Copilot coding agent, the resulting PR triggers the reviewer. Loose coupling all the way down. That's the whole trick, and it's also why Peli's factory scales to 100+ workflows without collapsing.

The concrete chain for spec → ship → review looks like this:

Spec agent (on: issues.opened, label needs-spec) reads a rough idea, rewrites it as a structured spec with acceptance criteria, posts it back on the issue, swaps the label to needs-plan.
Planner agent (on: issues.labeled [needs-plan]) breaks the spec into a task list, files sub-issues via create-issue, adds ready-for-implementation to each.
Implementer handoff (on: issues.labeled [ready-for-implementation]) uses the assign-to-agent safe output to hand the sub-issue to Copilot's cloud coding agent. This is the one step where real code gets written, and it's deliberately not a gh-aw agent because Copilot coding agent is the right tool for multi-file edits with CI feedback loops.
Reviewer agent (on: pull_request.opened) reads the diff, checks it against the original spec (pulled from the parent issue), posts a structured review, labels the PR ai-reviewed or needs-changes.
Gatekeeper agent (optional, on: pull_request.labeled [needs-changes]) pings the author on Slack via MCP, or re-assigns back to Copilot coding agent for a fix pass.
Three things that will bite you if you don't plan for them:

State between phases lives in issues, not memory. Each agent starts cold. The spec must be written back to the issue body or a comment so the planner can read it. Use repo-memory only for genuinely cross-run state like "which issues have I already seen." Issues are your database.

The review loop is where most factories fail. If your reviewer agent is too strict you get infinite rework loops; too loose and it's theater. Budget real time to tune the reviewer's prompt against 20-30 real PRs before you trust it. This is harness engineering work, not prompt work.

Non-determinism means you need a human circuit breaker. Add a human-review label that halts the chain at any step. The factory should be pauseable by any developer who sees it going sideways. Peli's team calls this the "emergency stop," and every production chain has one.

No reason at all. And your question is pointing at something I should have flagged before I built the port: committing your skills directory directly into the target repo is simpler than what I just did.

Here's the mechanics:

Claude Code and Codex engines auto-discover skills. Both scan the filesystem for SKILL.md files at runtime. Claude Code reads from .claude/skills/ and similar locations. Codex scans .agents/skills/ from cwd up to repo root. If you commit skills/ into the target repo and use either engine, the skills light up with zero porting.

Copilot is the outlier. It has no native skill discovery. It reads AGENTS.md and .github/copilot-instructions.md and that's it. So for Copilot you either inline the skill content (what I did) or reference the skill files from AGENTS.md and let Copilot's file-reading tools pull them in on demand.

Three caveats regardless of engine:

Skills with scripts need matching bash allowlists. Your self-improvement skill has shell scripts in scripts/. For those to run inside gh-aw, the workflow frontmatter has to include those commands in the bash: allowed: block. Instruction-only skills are free.
Skills with MCP servers need frontmatter declarations. If a skill bundles an MCP server, gh-aw won't auto-wire it. You declare it in the workflow's mcp-servers: block like we did for DX data.
Prompt injection surface. Skills get loaded into the agent's context as instructions. In a TV 2 internal repo where the platform team owns the skills, this is fine. In a public repo accepting contributions, it's a vector.

# AGENTS.md

Shared context for all agentic workflows in this repository. Every agent reads this file at run start.

## Who you are working for

TV 2 Denmark's developer platform team. We operate at the intersection of platform engineering, developer experience, and AI agent tooling. Our users are the internal engineering teams who build and ship TV 2's streaming and broadcast products.

## Core principles

1. **Move forward, fail fast, fail forward.** Do not stall on ambiguity. Make the best decision with the information available, document the assumption, and keep moving.
2. **Knowledge is for sharing.** When you learn something non-obvious, write it down in `.learnings/` so the next agent does not repeat the mistake.
3. **Skills are the new software.** Treat instructions as code. Version them, review them, improve them over time.
4. **Harness engineering is the differentiator.** The prompt is never the bottleneck. The structure around the prompt is.

## Skill discovery

This repository vendors reusable agent skills from [pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills](https://github.com/pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills) into the `skills/` directory. Every skill follows the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification):

```
skills/
  skill-name/
    SKILL.md         # Instructions + YAML frontmatter
    scripts/         # Optional executable code
    references/      # Optional reference material loaded on demand
    assets/          # Optional templates and data files
```

When a workflow tells you to use a skill, read `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` in full and follow its process. If the skill references additional files in `references/` or `assets/`, read those on demand as the skill instructs.

Currently vendored skills:
- `skills/plan-interview/`: structured requirements interview before planning
- `skills/dx-data-navigator/`: DX Data Cloud queries for DORA metrics and PR analytics
- `skills/self-improvement/`: learning capture and prevention rule promotion
- `skills/intent-framed-agent/`: explicit intent contract to prevent scope drift
- `skills/context-surfing/`: context window health monitoring with clean exits

## Adapting skills for single-shot gh-aw runs

The skills in this repo were originally written for live agent sessions with Claude Code, Codex CLI, or GitHub Copilot CLI. gh-aw runs are single-shot and ephemeral. When a skill assumes interactivity or cross-turn state that gh-aw cannot provide, follow these rules:

1. **Interview-style skills**: When a skill expects to ask the user questions, simulate the interview by answering from available context (issue body, linked PRs, repo files). Mark any answer you cannot give with confidence using `**NEEDS HUMAN INPUT**` and a specific question, then route to `blocked-on-human` via labels.
2. **Hook-based skills**: gh-aw has no PostToolUse or UserPromptSubmit hooks. When a skill expects hook activation, apply its logic at natural phase boundaries in your run (after planning, after major tool calls, before exit).
3. **Session-state skills**: Skills that monitor context window health or track state across turns cannot observe gh-aw runs directly. Apply their discipline as self-checks: read the skill, enumerate its checks, and run each one manually before committing output.
4. **Script-bundled skills**: If a skill has scripts in `scripts/`, those scripts must be explicitly allowlisted in the workflow frontmatter's `bash: allowed:` block. Instruction-only skills work everywhere with no configuration.

## Writing style for all agent-authored content

These rules apply to every comment, issue body, PR description, and commit message you produce.

- Never use em-dashes or double dashes. Use commas, colons, or periods.
- No "most teams" generalizations.
- No throat-clearing opening sentences. Lead with the answer.
- Short sentences. Strong declarative statements.
- If you quote data, link to the source.

## Spec and plan files

Plans live in `docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md` where NNN is a three-digit zero-padded sequence. The format is defined in `skills/plan-interview/SKILL.md`. Downstream agents use these files as the source of truth for implementation and review.

## Learnings

Learnings live in `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md` and follow this format:

```
## [LRN-NNN] Short title

**Status**: pending | promoted_to_skill | regressed
**Priority**: low | medium | high
**Area**: backend | frontend | infra | ci | docs | process
**Pattern-Key**: <stable-dedupe-key>
**Discovered**: YYYY-MM-DD via <workflow-run-url>

### What went wrong
[One paragraph]

### Root cause
[One paragraph]

### Prevention rule
[One short, checkable rule written in the imperative]

### See also
- LRN-XXX
```

Never log secrets, tokens, private keys, or full source files. Prefer short summaries over raw output. The full specification of this format lives in `skills/self-improvement/SKILL.md`.

## Agent routing guidelines

As of April 2026, GitHub offers three cloud coding agents, all bundled with the Copilot subscription: Copilot cloud agent, Claude (Sonnet 4.5/4.6, Opus 4.5/4.6), and Codex (GPT-5.2/5.3/5.4-Codex). Model selection happens when a task is kicked off on github.com. For workflows in this pack, `spec-refiner` recommends an implementer in the plan file, and a human confirms the assignment via the web UI.

Use these rules when recommending or choosing an implementer:

**Claude Opus 4.6**: default for complex, multi-file, or architecturally risky work
- Multi-file refactors touching more than three modules
- Plan files with `Blast radius: high`
- Anything with a non-trivial rollback path
- Plan files with more than six items in the implementation checklist
- Work that needs precise spec adherence because drift would matter

**Claude Sonnet 4.6**: default for straightforward single-component features
- Single-module feature additions with clear scope
- New API endpoints with existing patterns to follow
- Plan files with `Blast radius: medium`
- Bug fixes that require moderate investigation
- Anything where Opus would be overkill but you still want Claude's reasoning

**Copilot cloud agent**: default for trivial or highly-constrained work
- Dependency version bumps
- Obvious one-line fixes where the fix is already in the issue body
- Config file updates
- Repetitive mechanical changes across many files
- Plan files with `Blast radius: low` and a checklist under three items

**Codex (GPT-5.4)**: opportunistic use for specific strengths
- Tasks that benefit from a different reasoning style as a sanity check on Claude
- When the team wants A/B data on agent quality

### Why Claude is the default for non-trivial work at TV 2

The skills in `skills/` were originally designed for Claude Code. Running them on their native runtime gives better fidelity than any translation layer. The `plan-interview` structure, the intent framing discipline, the simplify-and-harden pass, all of it was tuned against Claude's reasoning patterns.

### How the recommendation gets made

`spec-refiner` adds a `## Recommended implementer` section to every plan file. It assesses the plan against the routing rules above and writes one of: `claude-opus-4.6`, `claude-sonnet-4.6`, `copilot`, or `codex-gpt-5.4`, with a one-line rationale. The human who reviews the plan PR sees the recommendation and decides whether to follow it when assigning sub-issues.

### A note on gh-aw engine selection

The routing rules above are about the **implementer step** (who writes the code from a sub-issue). The gh-aw engine that runs the workflows in this pack (`spec-refiner`, `tv2-reviewer`, `self-improvement-meta`) is a separate choice in each workflow's frontmatter. All workflows here currently use Copilot as the engine because it is bundled with the existing `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret. When gh-aw supports running the Claude engine through the same bundled subscription (expected soon based on the April 2026 changelog), flipping these workflows to `engine: claude` will be a one-line change per workflow.

## Tooling available to agents in this repo

- GitHub toolset (read-only by default, write via safe-outputs only)
- `cache-memory` and `repo-memory` for cross-run state
- DX Data Cloud MCP server at `https://dx-mcp.tv2.dk/mcp` (configured per workflow that needs it). Reviewer agents should use this for context.

## Human circuit breaker

Any workflow can be halted by adding the `human-review` label to the issue or PR it is operating on. When you see this label, call `noop` immediately and explain what you would have done.

[None, or findings]

---

# AI Proficiency Assessment for Pull Requests

Assess the repository's AI coding proficiency and context engineering maturity when PRs are opened or when someone comments `/assess-proficiency`.

## Trigger Conditions

Only run this assessment when:
1. A new pull request is opened or updated
2. Someone comments `/assess-proficiency` on a PR or issue

If triggered by a comment, check if the comment body contains `/assess-proficiency`. If not, exit without action.

## Assessment Process

### Step 1: Install the Tool

```bash
pip install measure-ai-proficiency
```

### Step 2: Run the Assessment

Run the proficiency scanner on the repository:

```bash
measure-ai-proficiency --format json --output proficiency-report.json
```

Also generate a markdown report:

```bash
measure-ai-proficiency --format markdown --output proficiency-report.md
```

### Step 3: Analyze the Results

Read the JSON report and extract:
- Overall maturity level (1-8)
- Total files detected at each level
- Top recommendations for improvement

### Step 4: Check for Context Engineering Changes in the PR

Look at the files changed in this PR. Identify any context engineering artifacts being added or modified:
- CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules
- ARCHITECTURE.md, CONVENTIONS.md, PATTERNS.md
- .github/copilot-instructions.md
- .claude/skills/, .claude/commands/, .claude/hooks/
- Any .md files in docs/

If context files are being added, this is positive - acknowledge the improvement.

### Step 5: Create the PR Comment

Post a comment on the PR with the following structure:

```markdown
## AI Proficiency Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **Overall Level** | Level X: [Name] |
| **Overall Score** | XX.X/100 |
| **Files Detected** | XX context files |

### Level Breakdown

[Include level-by-level breakdown with file counts]

### This PR's Impact

[Note any context engineering files being added/modified in this PR]

### Top Recommendations

[List the top 3 most impactful recommendations from the report]

---
*Powered by [measure-ai-proficiency](https://github.com/pskoett/measuring-ai-proficiency)*
```

## Important Guidelines

- Be constructive and encouraging, not critical
- Highlight any positive changes in the PR
- Keep recommendations actionable and specific
- If the repo is already at Level 4+, congratulate them and suggest advanced improvements
- If at Level 1, be encouraging about starting the journey

```

measure-ai-proficiency --format json --output proficiency-report.json
measure-ai-proficiency --format markdown --output proficiency-report.md

**Repository:** [Repo Name]

# Agents

This document defines agent roles and behavioral guidelines for AI assistants working on the measure-ai-proficiency project.

## Agent Roles

### Code Implementer

**Purpose:** Implement features, fix bugs, and maintain the codebase.

**Key behaviors:**
- Follow pure Python conventions (no external dependencies for core functionality)
- Use type hints on all functions and methods
- Use dataclasses for data structures
- Maintain backwards compatibility with Python 3.9+
- Run `pytest tests/ -v` before committing changes

**Files to modify:**
- `measure_ai_proficiency/scanner.py` - Core scanning logic
- `measure_ai_proficiency/config.py` - Level definitions and patterns
- `measure_ai_proficiency/reporter.py` - Output formatting
- `measure_ai_proficiency/repo_config.py` - Configuration handling
- `measure_ai_proficiency/github_scanner.py` - GitHub CLI integration

### Documentation Writer

**Purpose:** Keep documentation accurate and helpful.

**Key behaviors:**
- Update README.md when features change
- Keep docs/CUSTOMIZATION.md current with config options
- Sync skill files across all locations when updating:
  - `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`
  - `.github/skills/*/SKILL.md`
  - `skill-template/*/SKILL.md`
- Update `.ai-proficiency.yaml.example` when adding config options

**Constraints:**
- Never add features to docs that don't exist in code
- Always include examples with documentation
- Keep the example output in README.md current

### Skill Developer

**Purpose:** Create and maintain agent skills for this tool.

**Key behaviors:**
- Skills should be self-contained and follow the Agent Skills standard
- Include clear triggers and workflow steps
- Test skills work with both Claude Code and GitHub Copilot
- Sync skills to all three locations after changes

**Available skills:**
- `measure-ai-proficiency` - Run assessments
- `customize-measurement` - Configure for specific repos
- `plan-interview` - Interview-based planning
- `agentic-workflow` - GitHub agentic workflow creation

### Reviewer

**Purpose:** Review changes for quality and consistency.

**Key behaviors:**
- Verify type hints are present
- Check for backwards compatibility
- Ensure tests pass
- Validate documentation is updated
- Check skill files are synced across locations

## Behavioral Guidelines

### All Agents

1. **Test before committing:** Always run `pytest tests/ -v`
2. **Keep skills synced:** Changes to skills must be copied to all three locations
3. **Update version:** Bump version in `pyproject.toml` for releases
4. **Document config options:** New options go in:
   - `repo_config.py` (implementation)
   - `docs/CUSTOMIZATION.md` (documentation)
   - `.ai-proficiency.yaml.example` (example)
   - Skills that use the option

### Exit Codes

Maintain these exit codes:
- `0` - Success
- `1` - No repositories found
- `2` - All repositories at Level 1 (no AI context)

### Scoring System

When modifying scoring:
- Minimum scores per level: L2=15, L3=30, L4=45, L5=55, L6=70, L7=85, L8=95
- Validation penalty: max -4 points
- Cross-reference bonus: max +5 points
- Quality bonus: max +5 points

### Pattern Detection

When adding new patterns:
- Add to appropriate level in `config.py`
- Consider tool-specific filtering (Claude, Copilot, Cursor, Codex)
- Update KNOWN_TARGETS if it's an instruction file
- Add to INSTRUCTION_FILES if it should be scanned for cross-references

## Handoffs

### Implementation to Documentation
After implementing a feature, hand off to documentation:
- Describe what was added/changed
- Note any new config options
- List affected files

### Documentation to Skills
After updating documentation, update skills:
- measure-ai-proficiency skill for assessment features
- customize-measurement skill for config options

1	---
2	description: GitHub Agentic Workflows
3	applyTo: ".github/workflows/*.md,.github/workflows/**/*.md"
4	---
5	
6	# GitHub Agentic Workflows
7	
8	## File Format Overview
9	
10	Agentic workflows use a **markdown + YAML frontmatter** format:
11	
12	```markdown
13	---
14	on:
15	  issues:
16	    types: [opened]
17	permissions:
18	  issues: write
19	timeout-minutes: 10
20	safe-outputs:
21	  create-issue: # for bugs, features
22	  create-discussion: # for status, audits, reports, logs
23	---
24	
25	# Workflow Title
26	
27	Natural language description of what the AI should do.
28	
29	Use GitHub context expressions like ${{ github.event.issue.number }}.
30	```
31	
32	## Compiling Workflows
33	
34	**⚠️ IMPORTANT**: After creating or modifying a workflow file, you must compile it to generate the GitHub Actions YAML file.
35	
36	Agentic workflows (`.md` files) must be compiled to GitHub Actions YAML (`.lock.yml` files) before they can run:
37	
38	```bash
39	# Compile all workflows in .github/workflows/
40	gh aw compile
41	
42	# Compile a specific workflow by name (without .md extension)
43	gh aw compile my-workflow
44	```
45	
46	**Compilation Process:**
47	- `.github/workflows/example.md` → `.github/workflows/example.lock.yml`
48	- Include dependencies are resolved and merged
49	- Tool configurations are processed
50	- GitHub Actions syntax is generated
51	
52	**Additional Compilation Options:**
53	```bash
54	# Compile with strict security checks
55	gh aw compile --strict
56	
57	# Remove orphaned .lock.yml files (no corresponding .md)
58	gh aw compile --purge
59	
60	# Run security scanners
61	gh aw compile --actionlint  # Includes shellcheck
62	gh aw compile --zizmor      # Security vulnerability scanner
63	gh aw compile --poutine     # Supply chain security analyzer
64	
65	# Strict mode with all scanners
66	gh aw compile --strict --actionlint --zizmor --poutine
67	```
68	
69	**Best Practice**: Always run `gh aw compile` after every workflow change to ensure the GitHub Actions YAML is up to date.
70	
71	## Complete Frontmatter Schema
72	
73	The YAML frontmatter supports these fields:
74	
75	### Core GitHub Actions Fields
76	
77	- **`on:`** - Workflow triggers (required)
78	  - String: `"push"`, `"issues"`, etc.
79	  - Object: Complex trigger configuration
80	  - Special: `slash_command:` for /mention triggers (replaces deprecated `command:`)
81	  - **`forks:`** - Fork allowlist for `pull_request` triggers (array or string). By default, workflows block all forks and only allow same-repo PRs. Use `["*"]` to allow all forks, or specify patterns like `["org/*", "user/repo"]`
82	  - **`stop-after:`** - Can be included in the `on:` object to set a deadline for workflow execution. Supports absolute timestamps ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") or relative time deltas (+25h, +3d, +1d12h). The minimum unit for relative deltas is hours (h). Uses precise date calculations that account for varying month lengths.
83	  - **`reaction:`** - Add emoji reactions to triggering items
84	  - **`manual-approval:`** - Require manual approval using environment protection rules
85	
86	- **`permissions:`** - GitHub token permissions
87	  - Object with permission levels: `read`, `write`, `none`
88	  - Available permissions: `contents`, `issues`, `pull-requests`, `discussions`, `actions`, `checks`, `statuses`, `models`, `deployments`, `security-events`
89	
90	- **`runs-on:`** - Runner type (string, array, or object)
91	- **`timeout-minutes:`** - Workflow timeout (integer, has sensible default and can typically be omitted)
92	- **`concurrency:`** - Concurrency control (string or object)
93	- **`env:`** - Environment variables (object or string)
94	- **`if:`** - Conditional execution expression (string)
95	- **`run-name:`** - Custom workflow run name (string)
96	- **`name:`** - Workflow name (string)
97	- **`steps:`** - Custom workflow steps (object)
98	- **`post-steps:`** - Custom workflow steps to run after AI execution (object)
99	- **`environment:`** - Environment that the job references for protection rules (string or object)
100	- **`container:`** - Container to run job steps in (string or object)
101	- **`services:`** - Service containers that run alongside the job (object)
102	
103	### Agentic Workflow Specific Fields
104	
105	- **`description:`** - Human-readable workflow description (string)
106	- **`source:`** - Workflow origin tracking in format `owner/repo/path@ref` (string)
107	- **`labels:`** - Array of labels to categorize and organize workflows (array)
108	  - Labels filter workflows in status/list commands
109	  - Example: `labels: [automation, security, daily]`
110	- **`metadata:`** - Custom key-value pairs compatible with custom agent spec (object)
111	  - Key names limited to 64 characters
112	  - Values limited to 1024 characters
113	  - Example: `metadata: { team: "platform", priority: "high" }`
114	- **`github-token:`** - Default GitHub token for workflow (must use `${{ secrets.* }}` syntax)
115	- **`roles:`** - Repository access roles that can trigger workflow (array or "all")
116	  - Default: `[admin, maintainer, write]`
117	  - Available roles: `admin`, `maintainer`, `write`, `read`, `all`
118	- **`bots:`** - Bot identifiers allowed to trigger workflow regardless of role permissions (array)
119	  - Example: `bots: [dependabot[bot], renovate[bot], github-actions[bot]]`
120	  - Bot must be active (installed) on repository to trigger workflow
121	- **`strict:`** - Enable enhanced validation for production workflows (boolean, defaults to `true`)
122	  - When omitted, workflows enforce strict mode security constraints
123	  - Set to `false` to explicitly disable strict mode for development/testing
124	  - Strict mode enforces: no write permissions, explicit network config, pinned actions to SHAs, no wildcard domains
125	- **`features:`** - Feature flags for experimental features (object)
126	- **`imports:`** - Array of workflow specifications to import (array)
127	  - Format: `owner/repo/path@ref` or local paths like `shared/common.md`
128	  - Markdown files under `.github/agents/` are treated as custom agent files
129	  - Only one agent file is allowed per workflow
130	  - See [Imports Field](#imports-field) section for detailed documentation
131	- **`mcp-servers:`** - MCP (Model Context Protocol) server definitions (object)
132	  - Defines custom MCP servers for additional tools beyond built-in ones
133	  - See [Custom MCP Tools](#custom-mcp-tools) section for detailed documentation
134	
135	- **`tracker-id:`** - Optional identifier to tag all created assets (string)
136	  - Must be at least 8 characters and contain only alphanumeric characters, hyphens, and underscores
137	  - This identifier is inserted in the body/description of all created assets (issues, discussions, comments, pull requests)
138	  - Enables searching and retrieving assets associated with this workflow
139	  - Examples: `"workflow-2024-q1"`, `"team-alpha-bot"`, `"security_audit_v2"`
140	
141	- **`secret-masking:`** - Configuration for secret redaction behavior in workflow outputs and artifacts (object)
142	  - `steps:` - Additional secret redaction steps to inject after the built-in secret redaction (array)
143	  - Use this to mask secrets in generated files using custom patterns
144	  - Example:
145	    ```yaml
146	    secret-masking:
147	      steps:
148	        - name: Redact custom secrets
149	          run: find /tmp/gh-aw -type f -exec sed -i 's/password123/REDACTED/g' {} +
150	    ```
151	
152	- **`runtimes:`** - Runtime environment version overrides (object)
153	  - Allows customizing runtime versions (e.g., Node.js, Python) or defining new runtimes
154	  - Runtimes from imported shared workflows are also merged
155	  - Each runtime is identified by a runtime ID (e.g., 'node', 'python', 'go')
156	  - Runtime configuration properties:
157	    - `version:` - Runtime version as string or number (e.g., '22', '3.12', 'latest', 22, 3.12)
158	    - `action-repo:` - GitHub Actions repository for setup (e.g., 'actions/setup-node')
159	    - `action-version:` - Version of the setup action (e.g., 'v4', 'v5')
160	  - Example:
161	    ```yaml
162	    runtimes:
163	      node:
164	        version: "22"
165	      python:
166	        version: "3.12"
167	        action-repo: "actions/setup-python"
168	        action-version: "v5"
169	    ```
170	
171	- **`jobs:`** - Groups together all the jobs that run in the workflow (object)
172	  - Standard GitHub Actions jobs configuration
173	  - Each job can have: `name`, `runs-on`, `steps`, `needs`, `if`, `env`, `permissions`, `timeout-minutes`, etc.
174	  - For most agentic workflows, jobs are auto-generated; only specify this for advanced multi-job workflows
175	  - Example:
176	    ```yaml
177	    jobs:
178	      custom-job:
179	        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
180	        steps:
181	          - name: Custom step
182	            run: echo "Custom job"
183	    ```
184	
185	- **`engine:`** - AI processor configuration
186	  - String format: `"copilot"` (default, recommended), `"custom"` (user-defined steps)
187	  - ⚠️ **Experimental engines**: `"claude"` and `"codex"` are available but experimental
188	  - Object format for extended configuration:
189	    ```yaml
190	    engine:
191	      id: copilot                       # Required: coding agent identifier (copilot, custom, or experimental: claude, codex)
192	      version: beta                     # Optional: version of the action (has sensible default)
193	      model: gpt-5                      # Optional: LLM model to use (has sensible default)
194	      max-turns: 5                      # Optional: maximum chat iterations per run (has sensible default)
195	      max-concurrency: 3                # Optional: max concurrent workflows across all workflows (default: 3)
196	      env:                              # Optional: custom environment variables (object)
197	        DEBUG_MODE: "true"
198	      args: ["--verbose"]               # Optional: custom CLI arguments injected before prompt (array)
199	      error_patterns:                   # Optional: custom error pattern recognition (array)
200	        - pattern: "ERROR: (.+)"
201	          level_group: 1
202	    ```
203	  - **Note**: The `version`, `model`, `max-turns`, and `max-concurrency` fields have sensible defaults and can typically be omitted unless you need specific customization.
204	  - **Custom engine format** (⚠️ experimental):
205	    ```yaml
206	    engine:
207	      id: custom                        # Required: custom engine identifier
208	      max-turns: 10                     # Optional: maximum iterations (for consistency)
209	      max-concurrency: 5                # Optional: max concurrent workflows (for consistency)
210	      steps:                            # Required: array of custom GitHub Actions steps
211	        - name: Run tests
212	          run: npm test
213	    ```
214	    The `custom` engine allows you to define your own GitHub Actions steps instead of using an AI processor. Each step in the `steps` array follows standard GitHub Actions step syntax with `name`, `uses`/`run`, `with`, `env`, etc. This is useful for deterministic workflows that don't require AI processing.
215	
216	    **Environment Variables Available to Custom Engines:**
217	    
218	    Custom engine steps have access to the following environment variables:
219	    
220	    - **`$GH_AW_PROMPT`**: Path to the generated prompt file (`/tmp/gh-aw/aw-prompts/prompt.txt`) containing the markdown content from the workflow. This file contains the natural language instructions that would normally be sent to an AI processor. Custom engines can read this file to access the workflow's markdown content programmatically.
221	    - **`$GH_AW_SAFE_OUTPUTS`**: Path to the safe outputs file (when safe-outputs are configured). Used for writing structured output that gets processed automatically.
222	    - **`$GH_AW_MAX_TURNS`**: Maximum number of turns/iterations (when max-turns is configured in engine config).
223	    
224	    Example of accessing the prompt content:
225	    ```bash
226	    # Read the workflow prompt content
227	    cat $GH_AW_PROMPT
228	    
229	    # Process the prompt content in a custom step
230	    - name: Process workflow instructions
231	      run: |
232	        echo "Workflow instructions:"
233	        cat $GH_AW_PROMPT
234	        # Add your custom processing logic here
235	    ```

621	- **`safe-inputs:`** - Define custom lightweight MCP tools as JavaScript, shell, or Python scripts (object)
622	  - Tools mounted in MCP server with access to specified secrets
623	  - Each tool requires `description` and one of: `script` (JavaScript), `run` (shell), or `py` (Python)
624	  - Tool configuration properties:
625	    - `description:` - Tool description (required)
626	    - `inputs:` - Input parameters with type and description (object)
627	    - `script:` - JavaScript implementation (CommonJS format)
628	    - `run:` - Shell script implementation
629	    - `py:` - Python script implementation
630	    - `env:` - Environment variables for secrets (supports `${{ secrets.* }}`)
631	    - `timeout:` - Execution timeout in seconds (default: 60)
632	  - Example:
633	    ```yaml
634	    safe-inputs:
635	      search-issues:
636	        description: "Search GitHub issues using API"
637	        inputs:
638	          query:
639	            type: string
640	            description: "Search query"
641	            required: true
642	          limit:
643	            type: number
644	            description: "Max results"
645	            default: 10
646	        script: |
647	          const { Octokit } = require('@octokit/rest');
648	          const octokit = new Octokit({ auth: process.env.GH_TOKEN });
649	          const result = await octokit.search.issuesAndPullRequests({
650	            q: inputs.query,
651	            per_page: inputs.limit
652	          });
653	          return result.data.items;
654	        env:
655	          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
656	    ```
657	
658	- **`slash_command:`** - Command trigger configuration for /mention workflows (replaces deprecated `command:`)
659	- **`cache:`** - Cache configuration for workflow dependencies (object or array)
660	- **`cache-memory:`** - Memory MCP server with persistent cache storage (boolean or object)
661	- **`repo-memory:`** - Repository-specific memory storage (boolean)
662	
663	### Cache Configuration
664	
665	The `cache:` field supports the same syntax as the GitHub Actions `actions/cache` action:
666	
667	**Single Cache:**
668	```yaml
669	cache:
670	  key: node-modules-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
671	  path: node_modules
672	  restore-keys: |
673	    node-modules-
674	```
675	
676	**Multiple Caches:**
677	```yaml
678	cache:
679	  - key: node-modules-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
680	    path: node_modules
681	    restore-keys: |
682	      node-modules-
683	  - key: build-cache-${{ github.sha }}
684	    path: 
685	      - dist
686	      - .cache
687	    restore-keys:
688	      - build-cache-
689	    fail-on-cache-miss: false
690	```
691	
692	**Supported Cache Parameters:**
693	- `key:` - Cache key (required)
694	- `path:` - Files/directories to cache (required, string or array)
695	- `restore-keys:` - Fallback keys (string or array)
696	- `upload-chunk-size:` - Chunk size for large files (integer)
697	- `fail-on-cache-miss:` - Fail if cache not found (boolean)
698	- `lookup-only:` - Only check cache existence (boolean)
699	
700	Cache steps are automatically added to the workflow job and the cache configuration is removed from the final `.lock.yml` file.
701	
702	### Cache Memory Configuration
703	
704	The `cache-memory:` field enables persistent memory storage for agentic workflows using the @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory MCP server:
705	
706	**Simple Enable:**
707	```yaml
708	tools:
709	  cache-memory: true
710	```
711	
712	**Advanced Configuration:**
713	```yaml
714	tools:
715	  cache-memory:
716	    key: custom-memory-${{ github.run_id }}
717	```
718	
719	**Multiple Caches (Array Notation):**
720	```yaml
721	tools:
722	  cache-memory:
723	    - id: default
724	      key: memory-default
725	    - id: session
726	      key: memory-session
727	    - id: logs
728	```
729	
730	**How It Works:**
731	- **Single Cache**: Mounts a memory MCP server at `/tmp/gh-aw/cache-memory/` that persists across workflow runs
732	- **Multiple Caches**: Each cache mounts at `/tmp/gh-aw/cache-memory/{id}/` with its own persistence
733	- Uses `actions/cache` with resolution field so the last cache wins
734	- Automatically adds the memory MCP server to available tools
735	- Cache steps are automatically added to the workflow job
736	- Restore keys are automatically generated by splitting the cache key on '-'
737	
738	**Supported Parameters:**
739	
740	For single cache (object notation):
741	- `key:` - Custom cache key (defaults to `memory-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.run_id }}`)
742	
743	For multiple caches (array notation):
744	- `id:` - Cache identifier (required for array notation, defaults to "default" if omitted)
745	- `key:` - Custom cache key (defaults to `memory-{id}-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.run_id }}`)
746	- `retention-days:` - Number of days to retain artifacts (1-90 days)
747	
748	**Restore Key Generation:**
749	The system automatically generates restore keys by progressively splitting the cache key on '-':
750	- Key: `custom-memory-project-v1-123` → Restore keys: `custom-memory-project-v1-`, `custom-memory-project-`, `custom-memory-`
751	
752	**Prompt Injection:**
753	When cache-memory is enabled, the agent receives instructions about available cache folders:
754	- Single cache: Information about `/tmp/gh-aw/cache-memory/`
755	- Multiple caches: List of all cache folders with their IDs and paths
756	
757	**Import Support:**
758	Cache-memory configurations can be imported from shared agentic workflows using the `imports:` field.
759	
760	The memory MCP server is automatically configured when `cache-memory` is enabled and works with both Claude and Custom engines.
761	
762	### Repo Memory Configuration
763	
764	The `repo-memory:` field enables repository-specific memory storage for maintaining context across executions:
765	
766	```yaml
767	tools:
768	  repo-memory:
769	```
770	
771	This provides persistent memory storage specific to the repository, useful for maintaining workflow-specific context and state across runs.

775	### Automatic GitHub Issue Creation

778	
779	```aw

782	permissions:
783	  contents: read      # Main job only needs minimal permissions
784	  actions: read
785	safe-outputs:
786	  create-issue:
787	    title-prefix: "[analysis] "
788	    labels: [automation, ai-generated]
789	---

792	
793	Analyze the latest code changes and provide insights.
794	Create an issue with your final analysis.
